title: Infinitely Many Primes ≡ 1 (mod 4)
description: Proves there are infinitely many primes congruent to 1 modulo 4 using an elementary argument based on Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares. Considers N = (2·(n+1)!)² + 1 and shows every odd prime factor p of N satisfies p ≡ 1 (mod 4), since -1 is a square mod p (Euler's criterion). Uses Mathlib's Nat.Prime.mod_four_ne_three_of_dvd_isSquare_neg_one. 5 theorems, 0 definitions, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The infinitude of primes $\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ was known to Euler in the 18th century and represents a significant step beyond the elementary infinitude of primes. Unlike the $\equiv 3$ case — where a simple product-mod-4 argument suffices — the $\equiv 1$ case requires Euler's criterion from the theory of quadratic residues: $-1$ is a quadratic residue mod $p$ if and only if $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. This criterion appears in Euler's work on quadratic forms circa 1750 and is also the foundation for Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares (primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ are exactly the primes expressible as $a^2 + b^2$). The full generalization to all arithmetic progressions $a \pmod{m}$ with $\gcd(a,m) = 1$ was achieved by Dirichlet in 1837 using L-functions — the first deployment of analytic methods in number theory. The present elementary proof establishes the special case $a=1, m=4$ without any analysis.
overview.problemStatement: Prove that for every $n : \mathbb{N}$, there exists a prime $p > n$ with $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. Equivalently, the set $\{p \in \mathbb{N} : p \text{ prime},\ p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}\}$ is infinite. The proof uses the specific number $N = (2 \cdot (n+1)!)^2 + 1$ and Euler's criterion for quadratic residues.
overview.text: The key lemma `prime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four`: if an odd prime $p$ divides $k^2 + 1$, then $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. Proof: $k^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ means $-1$ is a square in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, which Mathlib's `mod_four_ne_three_of_dvd_isSquare_neg_one` converts to $p \not\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$; since $p$ is an odd prime, $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. For the main theorem: $N = (2 \cdot (n+1)!)^2 + 1$ is odd (even$^2$ + 1) and $> 1$, so has an odd prime factor $p$. $p \neq 2$ since $N$ is odd. By the key lemma $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. If $p \leq n$ then $p \mid (n+1)!$, so $p \mid N - (2(n+1)!)^2 = 1$, contradicting primality.
overview.proofStrategy: `prime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four`: construct `IsSquare (-1 : ZMod p)` using $k$ as witness from $k^2 + 1 \equiv 0$, then apply Mathlib's `Nat.Prime.mod_four_ne_three_of_dvd_isSquare_neg_one`. Main theorem: contradiction for $p \leq n$ via `Nat.dvd_factorial` + `Nat.Prime.not_dvd_one`. Set-theoretic formulation via `Set.infinite_iff_exists_gt`.
keyInsights: $N = (2 \cdot (n+1)!)^2 + 1$ is the $p \equiv 1$ analogue of $4 \cdot (n+1)! - 1$ used for $p \equiv 3$: being a perfect square plus 1 forces all odd prime factors to satisfy $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
Euler's criterion is the essential bridge: $-1$ is a square mod $p$ if and only if $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, which distinguishes this argument from the purely congruential $p \equiv 3$ proof.

The proof is a Euclidean argument in disguise: the factorial construction guarantees no prime factor $\leq n$ can divide $N$ without also dividing 1, echoing Euclid's classical proof of infinitude of primes.

The $\equiv 1$ and $\equiv 3$ cases together establish infinitude for all non-trivial residue classes mod 4 by elementary means, illustrating how Dirichlet's theorem reduces to two distinct elementary arguments at level $m = 4$.

Primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ are exactly the primes that split in the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, i.e., primes expressible as $a^2 + b^2$. The quadratic residue condition $-1 \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times 2}$ is exactly the splitting condition in the extension $\mathbb{Q}(i)/\mathbb{Q}$.
prerequisites: Euler's criterion: $-1$ is a square mod $p$ iff $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ (for odd primes $p$)

conclusion.summary: Proves infinitely many primes $\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ via $N = (2 \cdot (n+1)!)^2 + 1$ and Euler's quadratic residue criterion. The formalization uses Mathlib's `Nat.Prime.mod_four_ne_three_of_dvd_isSquare_neg_one` and delivers 5 theorems, 0 axioms, 177 lines — a complete machine-verified proof of a result that historically required Euler's theory of quadratic forms.
conclusion.implications: The contrast between this proof and the companion $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ proof (which uses only product-mod-4 arithmetic) illustrates how the arithmetic complexity of Euclid-style arguments scales with the residue class. Together they formalize infinitude for all non-trivial residue classes mod 4 by elementary means. The quadratic residue machinery here is the same ingredient underlying Fermat's two-square theorem and the splitting of primes in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, making this proof a gateway to algebraic number theory.
openQuestions: Can Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares be formalized using similar Mathlib infrastructure: $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4 \iff p = a^2 + b^2$? (Mathlib.NumberTheory.SumTwoSquares has the pieces.)
Can Dirichlet's theorem for all arithmetic progressions be formalized in Lean 4 with a complete L-function proof, or only via elementary special cases?
Is there a Lean 4 proof that primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ have density $1/2$ among all primes (Dirichlet density / Chebotarev density theorem)?

Fermat's theorem characterizes primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) as exactly those expressible as a² + b²; the same Euler criterion used here is the key ingredient
Quadratic reciprocity generalizes Euler's criterion for -1 to characterize all quadratic residues; the -1 case used here is the simplest instance

sections.title: Imports and Mathematical Background
sections.summary: Imports Mathlib modules for prime number theory (Nat.Prime.Basic), factorials, ZMod arithmetic, and critically Mathlib.NumberTheory.SumTwoSquares which contains Euler's criterion for -1 being a quadratic residue. The module docstring explains the full proof strategy.

sections.title: Key Lemma: Odd Primes Dividing k² + 1 Are ≡ 1 (mod 4)
sections.summary: The mathematical core: prime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four proves that if an odd prime p divides k² + 1, then p ≡ 1 (mod 4). Uses ZMod to construct IsSquare(-1 : ZMod p) from the divisibility hypothesis, then applies Mathlib's Euler criterion lemma to conclude p ≢ 3 (mod 4), and finishes by casework on p % 4 ∈ {1, 3}.

sections.title: Helper: Odd Numbers > 1 Have Odd Prime Factors
sections.summary: exists_odd_prime_factor: every odd number > 1 has an odd prime factor. Uses Nat.exists_prime_and_dvd for existence, then shows the factor cannot be 2 (since 2 | n would contradict n being odd).

sections.title: Main Theorem: Infinitely Many Primes ≡ 1 (mod 4)
sections.summary: infinitely_many_primes_1_mod_4: for every n, there exists a prime p > n with p ≡ 1 (mod 4). Constructs N = (2·(n+1)!)² + 1, shows N is odd and > 1 (so has an odd prime factor p), applies the key lemma to get p ≡ 1 (mod 4), and derives p > n by contradiction (p ≤ n forces p | 1 via factorial divisibility).

sections.title: Equivalent Formulations: Set Infinite and No-Largest
sections.summary: Two immediate corollaries: primes_1_mod_4_infinite states the set of such primes is infinite (via Set.infinite_iff_exists_gt); no_largest_prime_1_mod_4 states there is no largest prime ≡ 1 (mod 4). Both follow directly from the main theorem.

sections.title: Concrete Verified Examples
sections.summary: Proves by decide that 5, 13, 17, 29, 37 are all prime and ≡ 1 (mod 4). These are the first five elements of OEIS A002144 (primes ≡ 1 mod 4), all expressible as sums of two squares: 5=1²+2², 13=2²+3², 17=1²+4², 29=2²+5², 37=1²+6².
